stem: If an algorithm is O(n) and takes 1 second for 1,000 items, roughly how long for 10,000 items?
explanation_after: O(n) = linear time. If input grows 10x, time grows 10x. 10,000 items = ~10 seconds. This is why you must predict if code will work at scale.

stem: Attention in a transformer is O(n²) where n = sequence length. If processing 512 tokens takes 1 unit of compute, how much does 2048 tokens take?
explanation_after: 2048/512 = 4x more tokens. O(n²) means compute grows by 4² = 16x. This quadratic scaling is why long-context models are so expensive.

stem: Which Big O notation describes constant time, where runtime does not grow with input size?
explanation_after: O(1) = constant time. Dictionary lookup is O(1). Accessing a list element by index is O(1). These operations don't get slower as data grows.

The inner loop runs n times for every one of the n iterations of the outer loop, giving n × n = n² total operations — O(n²). Nested loops over the same data are the classic pattern that produces quadratic time.

stem: Which of these operations is O(log n)?

options.text: Looking up a value by key in a dictionary
Finding an element in a sorted array using binary search
Checking every element of an unsorted list one by one
Multiplying two n×n matrices the naive way

explanation_after: Binary search halves the search space at every step, giving O(log n). Dictionary lookup is O(1), a linear scan is O(n), and naive matrix multiplication is O(n³). Recognising log n growth matters because it barely increases even as the data doubles.

stem: A k-nearest-neighbours (k-NN) classifier makes a prediction by computing the distance from the query point to all n points in the training set, then picking the closest k. What is the time complexity of a single prediction, and why does this matter for deploying k-NN on a dataset of 10 million examples?

options.text: O(1) — k-NN just looks up the answer instantly
O(log n) — like binary search, distances can be found by halving the data
O(n) — every prediction scans all training data, so predictions get slower as the dataset grows, unlike models that learn a fixed set of parameters
O(n²) — because every point is compared to every other point

explanation_after: Unlike a trained model with a fixed number of parameters (e.g. logistic regression: O(d) per prediction regardless of training set size), k-NN keeps the entire training set and computes a distance to every point at prediction time — O(n) per query. With 10 million examples, every single prediction becomes slow. This is why Big-O reasoning directly drives the choice between 'lazy' algorithms like k-NN and 'eager' trained models in production systems.
